q: In the phospholipid bilayer, which part of each phospholipid faces the watery fluid on either side of the membrane?
options: The fatty acid tails
The phosphate heads
A cholesterol ring bonded to each tail
A sugar chain at the end of each tail

q: A researcher makes an artificial membrane that is a pure phospholipid bilayer, with no proteins. Which substance crosses it most easily?
options: Sodium ions
Glucose
Oxygen
Potassium ions

q: Which of these are jobs done by membrane proteins? Select all that apply.
options: Giving specific ions a path across the membrane
Forming the oily core that blocks ions
Speeding up reactions at the cell surface
Carrying sugar chains that mark the cell's identity
Storing the cell's genetic instructions

q: A blood sample from Mr. Tan sat for four hours before testing and was shaken hard. The lab reports plasma potassium of 6.8 mmol/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0), and the plasma looks pink. A fresh sample reads 4.1. What best explains the first result?
options: His kidneys stopped removing potassium between the two draws
Burst red blood cells spilled their potassium into the plasma in the tube
Potassium moved out of the plasma and into the red blood cells
Platelets released sodium, which the machine read as potassium
misconception: the fluid inside and outside cells has the same composition

q: Which description fits the glycocalyx?
options: Sugar chains on the outer face of the membrane
A layer of fat just under the plasma membrane
A protein framework lining the inside of the membrane
A second bilayer wrapped around the outside of the cell

q: A researcher rinses a membrane with salt water. Several proteins wash off. One protein stays until the whole membrane is dissolved with detergent. What best explains why it stays?
options: It is held to the glycocalyx by sugar bonds
It sits loosely on the inner surface
Its hydrophobic region sits in the bilayer's oily core
It is made of lipid rather than amino acids

q: Put these layers in order, starting in the interstitial fluid and moving into the cell.
options: Interstitial fluid
Glycocalyx
Phosphate heads of the outer sheet
Fatty acid tails
Phosphate heads of the inner sheet
Cytoplasm

q: Complete the path a glucose molecule takes from the blood into a cell: plasma inside a capillary → ______ → plasma membrane → cytoplasm.
options: Interstitial fluid
Intracellular fluid
The glycocalyx of a red blood cell
The nucleus

q: This sequence explains how a phospholipid bilayer forms. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Phospholipids are placed in water
Their hydrophilic heads attract water molecules
Their hydrophobic tails are drawn toward the water
The molecules form two sheets with their tails facing inward
The oily core between the sheets blocks ions

q: A fluid sample contains sodium at 142 mmol/L and potassium at 4.2 mmol/L. Which fluid could it be?
options: Cytoplasm from a red blood cell
Interstitial fluid
Fluid from inside a white blood cell
Intracellular fluid from any cell

q: Which of these fluids are part of the extracellular fluid? Select all that apply.
options: Plasma
Interstitial fluid
The watery part of the cytoplasm
The fluid inside a red blood cell
The fluid inside the nucleus

q: What does cholesterol do in the plasma membrane?
options: Lets ions cross the core
Forms the sugar coat on the outer face
Carries glucose into the cell
Steadies the membrane's fluidity as temperature shifts

q: A classmate says, "Once a phospholipid is in the plasma membrane, it stays in exactly that spot." Which observation shows this is wrong?
options: Phospholipids rarely flip from one sheet to the other
The glycocalyx is found only on the outer face
Integral proteins come out only when the bilayer is broken
Phospholipids keep drifting sideways, trading places within their sheet
misconception: the plasma membrane is a rigid wall

q: Ms. Oduya's blood count shows a very low number of platelets but normal red and white blood cells. Which problem is she most likely to notice?
options: Bleeding that is slow to stop after a small cut
Frequent infections that are slow to clear
Shortness of breath from poor oxygen delivery to tissues
A high potassium level in her plasma

q: Which part of the blood carries oxygen and, when mature, has no nucleus?
options: White blood cells
Platelets
Red blood cells
Plasma

q: A lab compares two sheets that both block sodium ions at first. One is plastic with tiny holes punched in it. The other is a living cell's plasma membrane. After a signal arrives, the cell's membrane starts letting sodium through, while the plastic sheet stays the same. What best explains the change?
options: Its phospholipids drifted apart and left open gaps
The signal made the oily core attract charged ions
The cell added transport proteins that let sodium cross
Sodium bound to the glycocalyx and was pulled through

q: A blood sample is shaken hard and many of its red blood cells burst in the tube. Predict each change in the tube.

variables.name: Potassium measured in the sample's plasma
Potassium in the patient's own bloodstream
Number of intact red blood cells in the tube

q: Which organelle has two membranes, the inner one folded into shelves, and makes most of a typical cell's ATP?
options: Golgi apparatus
Mitochondrion
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosome

q: A biopsy shows cells packed with rough ER and large Golgi stacks, with many vesicles near the surface facing a duct. What is these cells' main job most likely to be?
options: Exporting large amounts of protein
Making steroids
Absorbing nutrients through a brush border
Moving fluid across their surface

q: Which of these structures are built from microtubules? Select all that apply.
options: Cilia
The sperm flagellum
Centrioles
Microvilli
Intermediate filaments

q: A drug stops microtubules from forming. Which process in the cell is affected most directly?
options: The surface area provided by the brush border
Moving vesicles along tracks through the cytoplasm
Breakdown of hydrogen peroxide
Oxidation of fuel in mitochondria

q: Mr. Kowalski has been drinking heavily every day for months. His doctor notices that some of his medicines now wear off faster than expected. Which organelle has most likely increased in his liver cells?
options: Rough ER
Lysosomes
Golgi apparatus
Smooth ER

q: What is autophagy?
options: Recycling the cell's own worn-out parts
A cell dissolving after its lysosomes burst open
A ribosome building a protein for export
A mitochondrion dividing inside the cell

q: Put these steps in order for a digestive enzyme that a pancreas cell makes and releases.
options: A ribosome on the rough ER builds the protein
The protein is folded inside the rough ER
A vesicle carries the protein to the Golgi apparatus
The Golgi modifies and sorts the protein
A vesicle leaving the Golgi carries it to the plasma membrane
The vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases the enzyme

q: A few lysosomal enzymes leak into the cytosol of a healthy cell. Why do they cause little damage?
options: The cytosol has no proteins for them to act on
They work poorly at the near-neutral pH found in the cytosol
Catalase in the cytosol destroys them at once
Leaked enzymes are rebuilt into ribosomes straight away

q: Fill in the missing step: a very long fatty acid enters a peroxisome → peroxisome enzymes oxidize it, producing ______ → catalase breaks that product into water and oxygen.
options: Hydrogen peroxide
ATP
Glucose
Stored calcium ions

q: A cell's surface projections are about 1 micrometer long, have a core of actin, and never move. What are they, and what do they do?
options: Microvilli; they increase surface area
Cilia; they sweep fluid across the surface
Flagella; they move the cell
Microtubules; they carry vesicles
misconception: cilia and microvilli are the same structure

q: This sequence describes autophagy of a worn-out mitochondrion. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: A membrane wraps the worn-out mitochondrion
The wrapped package fuses with a lysosome
Lysosomal enzymes digest it at the neutral pH inside the lysosome
The mitochondrion is broken into small building blocks
The cell reuses the building blocks

q: Mr. Adeyemi, 31, has had chest and sinus infections all his life and has now been found to be infertile. Both problems trace to a single inherited defect. Which structure is most likely affected?
options: The actin core of the microvilli on airway cells
The digestive enzymes stored inside lysosomes
The microtubule core shared by cilia and flagella
The ribosomes on the rough ER

q: Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria. Which statement follows from that?
options: They cannot make ATP and rely on ATP from plasma
They make ATP in the cytosol instead
They get their ATP from enzymes inside lysosomes
They make their ATP on the rough ER instead

q: Which of these are part of the endomembrane system? Select all that apply.
options: Endoplasmic reticulum
Golgi apparatus
Lysosomes
Mitochondria
Free ribosomes

q: Which statement about mitochondria is most accurate?
options: They create new energy from the oxygen they take in
They store the body's reserve of ATP
They make energy without any fuel
They transfer energy from fuel into ATP

q: A drug stops a cell's lysosomes from keeping their interior acidic. Predict each change.

variables.name: Activity of the lysosomal enzymes
Recycling of worn-out organelles by autophagy
Amount of undigested material stored inside the cell

q: What is the cytosol?
options: The fluid part of the cytoplasm
All of the cytoplasm, including the organelles
The fluid that fills the spaces between cells
The fluid inside the endoplasmic reticulum

q: Which junction lets ions pass directly from the cytoplasm of one cell into the cytoplasm of its neighbor?
options: Tight junction
Desmosome
Gap junction
Glycocalyx

q: Mr. Lindqvist's skin blisters with light rubbing. A biopsy shows skin cells that have separated from each other, although each cell is intact. Which junction has most likely failed?
options: Gap junctions
Tight junctions
Microvilli
Desmosomes

q: Which proteins form the tunnels of a gap junction?
options: Connexins
Cadherins
Claudins
Actin subunits

q: A bacterial toxin loosens the tight junctions of the intestinal lining. What is the most direct result?
options: The cells pull apart and blister
Neighboring cells stop sharing ions through tunnels
Fluid and ions leak between the cells
The microvilli shrink

q: Which statements describe desmosomes? Select all that apply.
options: They anchor intermediate filaments
Cadherins cross the gap between the cells
They seal the space between cells
They let ions pass from cell to cell
They are abundant in skin and heart

q: Suppose every gap junction in the heart were blocked, while desmosomes and tight junctions stayed intact. What would change first?
options: The heart wall would tear apart
The heart's cells would stop contracting together
Blood would leak between the heart's cells
Each cell would stop making ATP

q: Put these steps in sequence to show how a sheet of skin cells resists a pull.
options: Friction pulls on one skin cell
The pull reaches the desmosome plaques in its membrane
Cadherins pass the pull across the gap to the neighboring cell
The neighbor's intermediate filaments take up the pull
The force spreads across many linked cells

q: Fill in the missing step: six connexins in one membrane form a ______ → it docks with a matching structure in the neighbor's membrane → a continuous tunnel links the two cytoplasms.
options: connexon
desmosome
plaque
tight junction strand

q: A medicine swallowed as a pill must cross the intestinal lining to reach the blood. Why must it pass through the lining cells rather than between them?
options: Desmosomes block every molecule
Gap junctions pull it into cells
Tight junctions seal the gaps
Microvilli trap it at the surface

q: This sequence describes what happens to gap junctions when a cell is badly injured. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: A cell is badly damaged
Calcium ions rise inside the damaged cell
Its connexons open wider
Ions stop passing between it and its neighbors
The healthy neighbors are sealed off from it

q: Which junction forms a continuous band all the way around a lining cell?
options: Desmosome
Tight junction
Gap junction cluster
Hemidesmosome

q: A child with inherited deafness is found to carry a defective form of one connexin. Which job is lost in the affected cells of the ear?
options: Riveting cells together against pulling
Sharing ions directly between neighboring cells
Sealing the spaces between cells
Anchoring cells to the layer below

q: Which of these can pass through a gap junction? Select all that apply.
options: Potassium ions
Glucose
ATP
A large protein
Water

q: A sheet of cells has intact tight junctions, but all its desmosomes are destroyed. What would you expect?
options: It leaks between cells but resists pulling
It stays sealed and resists pulling well
It leaks, and cells stop sharing ions
It stays sealed, but it tears easily when pulled
misconception: tight junctions are what hold cells together

q: Near the end of pregnancy, the number of gap junctions between cells in the uterine wall rises sharply. Predict each change.

variables.name: Flow of ions between neighboring uterine cells
How closely the cells contract together
Seal between the cells against leaks

q: Which of these would you expect to be richest in desmosomes?
options: Skin that is rubbed and stretched
Red blood cells floating in plasma
The urine held inside the bladder
White blood cells moving through tissue

q: Which substance crosses the plasma membrane by simple diffusion, with no protein involved?
options: Sodium ions
Carbon dioxide
Glucose molecules
Chloride ions

q: By mistake, a large volume of sterile water is infused into a patient's vein. What happens first to the red blood cells in the plasma it mixes with?
options: They shrink as water leaves them
They keep their normal size
They swell as water moves into them
They take in sodium from the water
misconception: any clear IV fluid is safe for blood cells

q: A red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic solution of sodium chloride. Predict each change in the cell.

variables.name: Volume of the cell
Concentration of solutes inside the cell
Number of potassium ions inside the cell

q: A cell takes up glucose on carrier proteins. Raising outside glucose from 1 to 2 mmol/L nearly doubles uptake, but raising it from 40 to 80 mmol/L barely changes it. What best explains this?
options: Glucose starts crossing the bilayer directly
The gradient reverses at high glucose
Nearly every carrier is already occupied by glucose
The carriers switch to moving other solutes
misconception: transport always speeds up with a bigger gradient

q: A membrane protein passes about 10 million potassium ions per second and almost no sodium ions. What kind of protein is it?
options: A potassium ion channel
A glucose carrier
An aquaporin
A glycoprotein in the glycocalyx

q: Which of these are forms of passive transport? Select all that apply.
options: Oxygen crossing the bilayer
Water entering a cell through aquaporins
Glucose entering a cell on a carrier, down its gradient
Fluid pushed out of a capillary by blood pressure
A cell spending ATP to move calcium from low to high concentration

q: A drug blocks every aquaporin in a red blood cell. The cell is then placed in a hypotonic solution. What happens?
options: Water cannot enter the cell by any route
It still swells, but more slowly
Water leaves the cell, and the cell shrinks
Ions rush in and replace the water

q: Put the steps of one cycle of a glucose carrier in sequence, starting with the carrier facing outside the cell.
options: Glucose from the interstitial fluid binds to the carrier's binding site
The carrier shifts shape so the binding site faces the cytoplasm
Glucose is released into the cytoplasm
The empty carrier flips back to face the outside

q: This sequence explains what happens to a red blood cell placed in a hypotonic solution. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The solution has fewer nonpenetrating solutes than the cell
The trapped solutes inside the cell cannot leave to even out
Water moves out of the cell by osmosis
The cell swells
If the swelling is severe, the membrane tears

q: Red blood cells (about 300 mOsm/L) are placed in a 300 mOsm/L solution of glycerol, a small molecule that crosses their membranes. What happens over the next few minutes?
options: They keep their volume
They shrink and crenate
They lose potassium but keep their volume
They swell and may burst

q: You step on a tack. The pressure deforms the membranes of touch-sensing nerve endings in the sole of your foot, and ion channels in them open. Which kind of channel opened?
options: A voltage-gated ion channel
A ligand-gated ion channel
A mechanically gated channel
A leak channel in the membrane

q: A channel in a muscle cell's membrane stays closed until a molecule released by the nerve that controls the muscle binds to it. What type of channel is this?
options: A mechanically gated channel
A ligand-gated channel
An aquaporin
A voltage-gated channel

q: Fill in the missing step: glucose binds to a carrier on the outside of the membrane → ______ → glucose is released into the cytoplasm.
options: The carrier changes shape
The carrier opens a tunnel all the way through
ATP attaches to the carrier and pushes glucose in
Glucose dissolves in the oily core of the bilayer

q: Two cells face the same glucose gradient. Cell A has twice as many glucose carriers as cell B. At very high outside glucose, how do their uptake rates compare?
options: They are equal, because the gradient is the same
Cell B is faster, because its carriers work harder
Cell A is about twice as fast
Neither takes up glucose once carriers saturate

q: Count only the pressure pushing fluid out, as in the filtration worked example. The pressure inside a patient's leg capillaries rises from 30 to 45 mm Hg because the veins draining them are partly blocked, and the pressure outside stays near 0. The capillary walls do not change. By this pressure-only reasoning, what happens to filtration out of those capillaries?
options: It falls by about half
It stays the same
It stops, because blood cells block the gaps
It rises by about half

q: An ion channel opens. Which of these decide the direction the ions move through it? Select all that apply.
options: The ion's concentration gradient across the membrane
The charge difference across the membrane
The trigger that opened the channel
The amount of ATP in the cell

q: Glucose enters a cell in your thigh muscle by facilitated diffusion, yet uptake continues for hours without the inside reaching the outside concentration. What keeps the gradient pointing inward?
options: The cell attaches a phosphate to each glucose as soon as it enters
Carriers let glucose in but block it from leaving
Aquaporins wash glucose into the cell with water
The cell spends ATP to push glucose through the carrier

q: What is crenation?
options: Swelling and bursting of a red blood cell in a hypotonic solution
Shrinking of a red blood cell in a hypertonic solution
The steady shape of a red blood cell in an isotonic solution
The opening of a channel when the membrane is stretched

q: Ms. Patel has dangerous swelling of her brain after a head injury. Her team infuses 3% sodium chloride into a vein. Sodium and chloride stay mostly outside brain cells. What effect does this have on her brain cells?
options: Water enters them and they swell further
Sodium enters them and they swell
Nothing changes, because saline is isotonic
Water leaves them and they shrink

q: For each ATP it splits, what does the sodium–potassium pump move?
options: 2 sodium ions out and 3 potassium ions in
3 sodium ions in and 2 potassium ions out
3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in
1 sodium ion out and 1 potassium ion in

q: Mr. Sato, 76, accidentally takes a large overdose of digoxin, which blocks sodium–potassium pumps. His plasma potassium rises to 6.5 mmol/L. What best explains the rise?
options: Digoxin carries potassium into the blood
Potassium is no longer pumped back into cells
His cells are now pumping extra potassium out into the plasma
Sodium is being converted into potassium

q: A poison completely blocks the sodium–potassium pumps of a cell that takes up glucose on a sodium–glucose symporter. Predict each change over the next hour.

variables.name: Sodium concentration inside the cell
Potassium concentration inside the cell
Cell volume
Glucose uptake by the symporter

q: Which of these is primary active transport?
options: A carrier moving glucose into a cell down its gradient
A carrier dragging glucose in with sodium
Water entering a cell through aquaporins
A calcium pump splitting ATP to push calcium out

q: A symporter in a kidney tubule cell carries glucose into the cell against its gradient but never splits ATP. Where does the energy for this uphill movement come from?
options: Sodium moving into the cell down its electrochemical gradient
Glucose moving down its own concentration gradient
Heat released by the kidney tubule
The pressure of fluid in the tubule
misconception: secondary active transport does not depend on ATP

q: A cell runs out of ATP. Which of these processes will stop, either at once or as gradients run down? Select all that apply.
options: The sodium–potassium pump
Glucose uptake on a sodium–glucose symporter
Oxygen diffusing across the bilayer
Endocytosis
Exocytosis

q: Put the steps of one sodium–potassium pump cycle in sequence, starting with the pump open toward the cytoplasm.
options: Three sodium ions from the cytoplasm bind to the pump
The pump splits ATP, and a phosphate stays attached to it
The pump changes shape and releases sodium outside the cell
Two potassium ions from outside bind to the pump
The phosphate is released, and the pump returns to its original shape
The pump releases potassium into the cytoplasm

q: This sequence describes the sodium–potassium pump. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Three sodium ions bind to the pump on the cytoplasm side
ATP is split and a phosphate attaches to the pump
The pump changes shape and releases sodium into the cytoplasm
Two potassium ions bind from the extracellular fluid
The phosphate comes off, and potassium is released into the cytoplasm

q: In a heart cell, a carrier lets three sodium ions in while pushing one calcium ion out. What kind of transport is this?
options: Symport, a form of passive transport
Primary active transport, using ATP split by the carrier
Antiport, a form of secondary active transport
Facilitated diffusion through a channel

q: Leo, 12, has a blood cholesterol level several times normal. His cells make normal cholesterol-carrying particles, but the surface proteins that should bind those particles are defective. Which process has failed?
options: Phagocytosis
Receptor-mediated endocytosis
Exocytosis
Simple diffusion of cholesterol

q: A white blood cell reaches out around a bacterium, encloses it in a vesicle, and delivers it to a lysosome. What is this process?
options: Pinocytosis
Phagocytosis
Exocytosis
Secondary active transport

q: Fill in the missing step: a vesicle carrying digestive enzymes moves to the plasma membrane → ______ → the enzymes are released outside the cell.
options: The vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane
A pump moves the enzymes across one at a time
The enzymes diffuse through the bilayer
The plasma membrane folds around the vesicle and pinches off

q: A pancreas cell releases enzymes by exocytosis thousands of times a minute, yet its surface area stays about the same. What best explains this?
options: The vesicles fuse without adding membrane
The extra membrane dissolves in the fluid outside
The cell grows larger with every release
Endocytosis removes membrane from the surface at a matching rate

q: A child with cholera, losing large amounts of water and salt through the gut, is given oral rehydration solution, which contains glucose as well as salt. Why does adding glucose help the child absorb sodium and water?
options: Glucose makes the gut contents hypertonic to the cells
Glucose blocks the sodium–potassium pump
Glucose opens aquaporins directly
Glucose and sodium enter on a shared symporter

q: A patient takes a drug that blocks the hydrogen–potassium pumps of the stomach lining. What happens to stomach acid?
options: It rises, because hydrogen ions build up in the stomach
It is unchanged, because hydrogen ions diffuse in anyway
It rises, because potassium replaces the hydrogen ions
It falls, because fewer hydrogen ions are pumped into the stomach

q: Which of these are true of the sodium–potassium pump but not of facilitated diffusion by a glucose carrier? Select all that apply.
options: It moves ions against their gradients
It splits ATP
It is an integral membrane protein
It binds its cargo and changes shape
It moves net positive charge out of the cell

q: What is pinocytosis?
options: A cell engulfing a whole bacterium
A cell taking in a small droplet of fluid
A vesicle releasing its contents outside the cell
A pump moving hydrogen ions into a lysosome

q: A cell's sodium–potassium pumps stop. The cell is then placed in a solution whose sodium concentration matches its cytoplasm, with the missing sodium replaced by a solute that cannot enter cells, so the osmolarity stays normal. Compared with a pump-blocked cell in normal extracellular fluid, how much does it swell?
options: Much more, because sodium now leaks in faster
Much less, because far less sodium leaks in
The same, because swelling depends only on ATP
Not at all, because the pumps are what cause swelling

q: Which statement describes exocytosis?
options: A vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside
The plasma membrane folds around material outside the cell and pinches it inward
A carrier uses the sodium gradient to move glucose into the cell
A pump splits ATP to move ions out of the cell

q: In a DNA double helix, which base pairs with guanine?
options: Adenine
Thymine
Cytosine
Another guanine

q: One DNA strand reads 5′-GATTCA-3′. Which sequence is its complementary partner strand, written with its ends labeled?
options: 3′-CTAAGT-5′
5′-CTAAGT-3′
3′-GATTCA-5′
3′-CUAAGU-5′

q: A sample of double-stranded human DNA is 22% thymine. What percentage of its bases is cytosine?
A genetic lab receives a tube of a patient's blood. The technician explains that almost all the DNA she extracts comes from a small fraction of the cells in the tube. Which cells supply the DNA?
options: Mature red blood cells
White blood cells
Platelets
Cells dissolved in the plasma

q: Select every structure that is part of the nucleus.
options: Nuclear envelope
Nucleolus
Chromatin
Golgi apparatus
Lysosome
Nuclear pores

q: Put the levels of DNA packing in order, from least packed to most packed.
options: Bare double helix
Nucleosomes: DNA wrapped around histone cores, like beads on a string
Coiled and looped chromatin fiber
Condensed chromosome in a dividing cell

q: One of your body cells has just finished copying all of its DNA and has not yet divided. How many chromosomes and how many chromatids does it contain?
options: 92 chromosomes and 92 chromatids
46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids

q: A student lists the steps of DNA replication. Which step contains the error?
options: Helicase separates the two strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
Free nucleotides pair with the exposed bases: A with T and G with C.
DNA polymerase links the new nucleotides into a strand and removes most wrongly placed bases.

q: Fill in the missing step. Helicase unwinds the helix and separates the strands → free nucleotides pair with the exposed bases → ______ → two identical double helices, each with one old and one new strand.
options: DNA polymerase joins the paired nucleotides into a new strand
Histones wrap each separated single strand into nucleosomes of its own

The nucleolus assembles the new strands

q: Researchers heat four DNA segments of equal length until their two strands separate. Which segment needs the highest temperature?
options: A segment that is 30% guanine plus cytosine
A segment that is 45% guanine plus cytosine
A segment that is 70% adenine plus thymine
A segment that is 65% guanine plus cytosine

q: Histone proteins are rich in amino acids that carry a positive charge. Why does DNA wrap tightly around them?
options: DNA's bases form hydrogen bonds with the histones
The negative phosphate backbone is drawn to the positive histones
DNA's sugars are hydrophobic and hide inside the histone core
Histones cut the DNA into short pieces that fit each core

q: Of the 23 pairs of chromosomes in most of your body cells, how many pairs are autosomes?
Bacteria are grown with nitrogen that makes their DNA heavy, then moved to ordinary nitrogen and allowed to copy their DNA exactly once. What will the new DNA molecules look like?
options: Half of the molecules fully heavy and half of them fully light
All molecules fully light, with the heavy strands discarded
All molecules still fully heavy on both strands

q: Compare a liver cell and a skin cell from the same person. Which statement about their DNA is accurate?

They carry the same genome, but each uses a different set of genes
The skin cell has fewer chromosomes than the liver cell
Each carries a different sequence of bases in the same genes

q: What is a gene?
options: A whole chromosome, from one end to the other
A single nucleotide within the DNA strand
A stretch of DNA whose base sequence codes for a working product
The histone core that DNA wraps around in a nucleosome

q: A cell is treated with a drug that blocks helicase just before it begins to copy its DNA. Predict the change in each variable compared with an untreated cell.

variables.name: Amount of separated, single-stranded DNA exposed
Amount of new DNA made
Number of chromosomes in the cell

q: A drug blocks transport through the nuclear pores. What would you expect to build up inside the nucleus?
options: Mitochondria from the cytoplasm
Lysosomes from the Golgi apparatus
Newly assembled ribosome halves
Glucose from the blood

q: Which feature is found in RNA but not in DNA?
options: The base thymine
Two strands wound into a double helix
The base uracil
The sugar deoxyribose

q: The template strand of a gene reads 3′-TACGGC-5′. What mRNA does RNA polymerase make from it?
options: 5′-ATGCCG-3′
5′-AUGCCG-3′
5′-UACGGC-3′
5′-TACGGC-3′

An mRNA reads 5′-AUG UUU GGC UAA-3′. Using AUG = methionine (start), UUU = phenylalanine, GGC = glycine and UAA = stop, what does a ribosome make?

Methionine alone

Every amino acid after that point changes
One amino acid is swapped for a different one

q: Two mutations hit the same gene near its start. One deletes a single base. The other deletes three neighboring bases that make up one codon. Which comparison is most accurate?

The three-base deletion shifts every later codon; the single-base deletion removes one amino acid

Trapped in the ER of his liver cells
In the nucleus, stuck behind the nuclear pores

q: A man eats wild mushrooms, and two days later he has signs of liver failure. The mushrooms contained a toxin that blocks the RNA polymerase that copies protein-coding genes. Which step fails first in his liver cells?

Reading mRNA codons on ribosomes
Copying DNA before the cell divides
Releasing proteins by exocytosis

q: Put the steps in order for a pancreas cell making a digestive enzyme and releasing it from the cell.
options: RNA polymerase transcribes the gene
The spliceosome removes introns and joins exons
The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore
A ribosome begins translation, and the new chain's signal sequence docks it on the rough ER

q: A student describes translation. Which step contains the error?

q: Pancreas cells make large amounts of a digestive enzyme, while skin cells from the same person make none. What best explains the difference?

Each ribosome makes one tenth of the whole protein

Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite ends
